b: Just like once I talked about the double standard considering men being drafted while liberal feminists want equality but don't want equal draft and how war was equally dangerous for men, here I post double standard which for me prioritizes men and not women.

I find the mainstream conversation about men's mental health somewhat selective. While men's struggles deserve attention, we rarely acknowledge that a white, Western man often has considerably more social and economic privilege than a Black, Latino, Middle Eastern or Punjabi immigrant man. Men's experiences are not universal, and race, class and immigration status matter.

I also question why so much responsibility for men's emotional well-being is placed on women. Women are frequently expected to provide emotional support, reassurance and unpaid therapeutic labour, while discussions about male loneliness sometimes become entangled with dating, romantic rejection and sexual access. Women are not responsible for resolving men's psychological difficulties, nor should relationships or sex be presented as solutions to them.

There also seems to be an imbalance in expectations - women are historically expected to understand, accommodate and emotionally support men, but comparable concern for women's psychological well-being and emotional needs is not always emphasised. Men's mental health deserves advocacy, but that advocacy should involve personal responsibility, accessible mental healthcare and genuine social support, not an expectation that women must compensate for what men lack emotionally.

Another issue is the apparent double standard in how society responds to violent crimes committed by men versus women, particularly when mental health is involved. Male perpetrators can sometimes receive considerable public sympathy, with their psychological struggles, trauma, relationship breakdowns or personal circumstances used to explain their behaviour, even in extremely brutal cases. Women who commit comparable crimes, however, are often portrayed as uniquely monstrous, irredeemable or inherently dangerous. Cases such as Jodi Arias and Lindsay Clancy raise questions about why female perpetrators so often receive substantially less understanding, particularly when discussions involve infidelity, relationship trauma or abusive family dynamics. This is not about excusing murder or glorifying female perpetrators; it is about questioning the inconsistency in how we interpret their circumstances.

There is also a disturbing contradiction in how women's mental health is treated before these tragedies occur. Warning signs and destructive behaviour can be trivialised through attitudes such as "crazy women are the best in bed" or "don't stick your dick in crazy", rather than taken seriously. At the same time, women experiencing severe psychological difficulties can still face enormous societal pressure to become wives and mothers, with dating/marriage and reproduction presented as obligations rather than choices. We cannot simultaneously dismiss women's psychological distress, trivialise their warning signs, pressure them into traditional roles and then act completely bewildered when situations escalate into tragedy. Prevention requires taking mental health seriously before it becomes a criminal matter, regardless of gender.
